kurals.tamil:
நில்லாத வற்றை நிலையின என்றுணரும்
புல்லறி வாண்மை கடை.
kurals.transliteration:
Nillaadha vatrai nilaiyina endru unarum
Pullarivu aanmai kadai.
kurals.meaning: To take things that cannot last and believe they are permanent is the lowest kind of foolishness.
kurals.elementary: Imagine building a sandcastle and believing it will stay on the beach forever, even though the waves always come. This kural says that treating things that will surely change or go away as if they will last forever is the silliest mistake a person can make.
kurals.university: Valluvar opens the chapter on impermanence not with a description of transience but with an epistemic judgement: the root error is a false cognition, mistaking the non-abiding (nillaadhavai) for the abiding (nilaiyina). The phrase “pullarivaanmai” (petty-mindedness, a paltry intelligence that presumes itself competent) frames the problem as a defect of understanding rather than of morals, and “kadai” (the lowest, the most base) ranks it at the bottom of human conditions. Commentators from Parimelazhagar onward read the chapter as the doorway of the renunciate section (thuravaraviyal), since recognising impermanence (nilaiyaamai) is what loosens attachment and makes renunciation (the next chapter, thuravu) intelligible. The idea sits close to the Buddhist and Jain analysis of avidya/moha, where suffering follows from treating the impermanent as permanent, and to the Stoic insistence that disturbance comes from our judgements about things rather than from the things themselves.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O son of Kunti, the contact between the senses and the sense objects gives rise to fleeting perceptions of happiness and distress. These are non-permanent, and come and go like the winter and summer seasons.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna that the pleasures and pains people cling to are passing like the seasons, and a wise person does not treat them as solid or lasting.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita labels these experiences anitya (non-permanent), which is the same diagnosis the Kural makes: the mistake is treating the non-lasting as lasting.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong thematic match on impermanence; the Gita stresses enduring sensations with equanimity, while the Kural stresses the error of believing them permanent.

christianity.quote_or_event: “While we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen: for the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells believers to fix their attention on what lasts rather than on visible things, which are only temporary.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural condemns mistaking the temporary for the permanent; Paul teaches the right way to tell the temporal from the eternal.
christianity._accuracy_note: Clear temporal/eternal distinction; Paul frames it in terms of faith and unseen realities, the Kural in terms of right knowledge.

islam.quote_or_event: “Everyone upon the earth will perish, And there will remain the Face of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honor.”
islam.explanation: The Quran says everything on earth will pass away and only God remains.
islam.tie_back: Only one thing truly abides, so treating anything worldly as permanent is exactly the error the Kural calls the lowest foolishness.
islam._accuracy_note: Direct statement of universal transience; the Quran contrasts it with the divine, which the Kural does not name here.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity.”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet (Ecclesiastes) opens by calling everything under the sun hevel, a breath or vapour that does not last.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts start from the same claim: worldly things are fleeting, and seeing them as solid is a mistake.
judaism._accuracy_note: Hevel (breath/vapour) captures transience well; Kohelet's tone is more one of weary puzzlement than the Kural's sharp moral ranking.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “All conditioned things are impermanent” — when one sees this with wisdom, one turns away from suffering. This is the path to purification.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha names impermanence (anicca) as a mark of all conditioned things; seeing it clearly frees a person from suffering.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's ‘lowest foolishness’ is the reverse of this wisdom: the fool sees permanence where the Buddha teaches there is only anicca.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match: both make correct perception of impermanence the key divide between wisdom and folly.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Eos, goddess of the dawn, asked Zeus to make her mortal lover Tithonus immortal but forgot to ask for eternal youth; he went on living while shrivelling with age until he could not move.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth shows the danger of assuming that what belongs to a mortal, like youth, can simply be made to last.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Eos treated youth as if it were permanent, the very mistake the Kural calls the lowest kind of understanding.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Illustrative rather than doctrinal: the myth dramatises a failure to reckon with impermanence but is not a teaching about it.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Heracleitus is supposed to say that all things are in motion and nothing at rest; he compares them to the stream of a river, and says that you cannot go into the same water twice.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates reports Heraclitus' view that everything is constantly changing, like a flowing river.
philosophy.tie_back: If everything flows, then believing things are fixed and permanent is exactly the misperception the Kural condemns.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong match on universal flux; Heraclitus offers a cosmology, while the Kural offers a moral verdict on those who ignore it.

kurals.tamil:
கூத்தாட்டு அவைக்குழாத் தற்றே பெருஞ்செல்வம்
போக்கும் அதுவிளிந் தற்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Koothaattu avaikkuzhaath thatre perunjelvam
Pokkum adhu vilindhatru.
kurals.meaning: Great wealth gathers the way a crowd gathers at a dance performance, and it leaves the way that crowd scatters when the show is over.
kurals.elementary: Think of people crowding in to watch a street show. When the show ends, everyone walks away at once and the place is empty. This kural says money is like that crowd: it comes in bit by bit, and it can leave all at once.
kurals.university: Valluvar builds the couplet on a single theatrical simile with two halves: the assembling of an audience (koothaattu avaik kuzhaam) and its dispersal when the performance ends (adhu vilindhatru). Commentators note the asymmetry the image implies: an audience trickles in gradually but leaves together, just as wealth is accumulated slowly and can vanish in a single reversal. The theatre is also suggestive, since the crowd was never attached to the patron but to the spectacle, much as wealth is never truly bound to its holder. The kural therefore relocates wealth from the category of possession to that of event, something that happens around a person for a time. Comparable ideas appear in the Greek theme of the reversal of fortune (Solon and Croesus) and in the Stoic teaching that external goods are on loan.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Offered wealth, long life, horses, and dancing and singing by Yama, the boy Nachiketas refuses, saying such things last only until tomorrow and wear out the senses, and tells Death to keep his dances and songs.
hinduism.explanation: In the Katha Upanishad, a young seeker rejects every worldly prize because it is short-lived and asks instead for knowledge of what lies beyond death.
hinduism.tie_back: Nachiketas sees wealth and entertainment for what the Kural says they are, a show that ends and a crowd that disperses.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Strong match on the fleeting nature of wealth, and the dance and song imagery even echoes the Kural's theatre; the Upanishad's stress is on choosing Self-knowledge instead.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy;”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells Timothy to warn the rich not to rely on wealth, because riches are uncertain.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Uncertain riches’ is the Kural's point in a phrase: wealth can leave as quickly as a crowd after a show.
christianity._accuracy_note: Direct match on the instability of wealth; Paul redirects trust to God, which the Kural does not explicitly do here.

islam.quote_or_event: “Know that the life of this world is but amusement and diversion and adornment and boasting to one another and competition in increase of wealth and children - like the example of a rain whose [resulting] plant growth pleases the tillers; then it dries and you see it turned yellow; then it becomes [scattered] debris.”
islam.explanation: The Quran compares worldly life and the race for wealth to entertainment and to crops that flourish and then dry up and scatter.
islam.tie_back: Both texts use the language of amusement and spectacle, and both say the gathering of wealth ends in scattering.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close: ‘amusement and diversion’ parallels the theatre image, and the growth-then-scattering arc matches the Kural's two halves.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Wilt thou set thine eyes upon that which is not? for riches certainly make themselves wings; they fly away as an eagle toward heaven.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs warns against fixing your gaze on riches, which suddenly grow wings and fly away.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's crowd scatters and Proverbs' riches fly off; both describe how suddenly wealth can leave.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close match: a vivid image of wealth's sudden departure, differing only in the metaphor used.

buddhism.quote_or_event: One who looks upon the world as a bubble and a mirage, him the King of Death sees not.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches seeing the world, and the things in it, as a bubble or mirage: real enough to appear, too fleeting to hold.
buddhism.tie_back: A bubble and a theatre crowd are both brief gatherings that vanish; the wise, in both texts, are not taken in by them.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good thematic parallel on transience, but the verse concerns the whole world rather than wealth specifically.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The Athenian sage Solon refused to call the fabulously rich King Croesus the happiest of men, saying no one should be called happy until his life has ended well. Croesus later lost his kingdom to Cyrus and, on the pyre, cried out Solon's name.
greek_mythology.explanation: Herodotus' story shows the richest man in the world losing everything in a single reversal.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Croesus' treasure gathered over a lifetime and scattered in a day, just as the Kural's crowd leaves when the show ends.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Greek legendary history rather than myth proper; a strong narrative illustration of wealth's sudden reversal.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Never say of anything, "I have lost it"; but, "I have returned it." ... Is your estate taken away? Well, and is not that likewise returned?”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus teaches that property is never truly ours: it is lent for a while and eventually given back.
philosophy.tie_back: If wealth is only on loan, its leaving is as natural as an audience going home after the show, which is the Kural's point.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Shares the insight that wealth is not truly possessed; Epictetus draws a lesson in equanimity rather than using a theatre simile.

kurals.tamil:
அற்கா இயல்பிற்றுச் செல்வம் அதுபெற்றால்
அற்குப ஆங்கே செயல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Arkaa iyalbitruch selvam adhu petraal
Arkupa aange seyal.
kurals.meaning: Wealth is by nature unstable; so when you have it, use it at once to do the good deeds that last.
kurals.elementary: If you are given ice cream on a hot day, you should share it right away before it melts. This kural says money is like that ice cream: it won't stay, so use it for good things now, while you still have it.
kurals.university: The couplet turns on a deliberate play between “arkaa” (that which does not stay) and “arkupa” (things that do stay, that is, enduring deeds), both drawn from the verb ‘ar’, to abide. Valluvar thus converts a descriptive claim about wealth into an imperative: since wealth is non-abiding, use it for what abides, and do so “aange” (then and there, at once). Commentators identify the enduring deeds with the householder virtues discussed earlier in the work, such as hospitality, charity and helpfulness (oppuravu). The logic is an ethical economics: a perishable asset should be exchanged immediately for an imperishable one before it spoils. The same move, turning transient riches into lasting merit, appears in the Gospel's ‘treasures in heaven’, the Quran's ‘enduring good deeds’, and Bhartrhari's teaching that wealth has only three destinies.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bhartrhari teaches that wealth has only three possible destinies: it is given away, it is enjoyed, or it is destroyed. Whoever neither gives nor enjoys it is left with the third.
hinduism.explanation: The Sanskrit poet says wealth that is not given away or used will simply be lost.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts start from wealth's instability and conclude that it should be turned into giving before it disappears.
hinduism.source: Bhartrhari, Nitishataka, v. 43 (numbering varies by edition)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Very close in logic: impermanent wealth should be given away before loss claims it. Bhartrhari also allows enjoyment, which the Kural does not stress.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal:”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his listeners to stop hoarding wealth that decays and to store up lasting treasure through a godly life.
christianity.tie_back: Swap perishable treasure for imperishable treasure: this is exactly the Kural's ‘arkaa’ turned into ‘arkupa’.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one structural match: perishable wealth should be converted into lasting merit.

islam.quote_or_event: “Wealth and children are [but] adornment of the worldly life. But the enduring good deeds are better to your Lord for reward and better for [one's] hope.”
islam.explanation: The Quran contrasts wealth, which is decoration for this life, with ‘al-baqiyat as-salihat’, good deeds that endure.
islam.tie_back: The Quran's ‘enduring good deeds’ are the Kural's ‘arkupa’ (things that last), set against wealth that does not.
islam._accuracy_note: Striking verbal parallel: the same contrast of transient wealth and enduring deeds; the Kural adds the note of urgency (‘at once’).

judaism.quote_or_event: “Riches profit not in the day of wrath: but righteousness delivereth from death.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs teaches that wealth is useless at the decisive moment, while righteousness (tzedakah, which also came to mean charity) saves.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts rank righteous action above wealth because only the former survives the final reckoning.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match on wealth's ultimate uselessness versus righteousness; lacks the Kural's explicit instruction to spend wealth on virtue immediately.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Truly, misers fare not to heavenly realms; nor, indeed, do fools praise generosity. But the wise man rejoices in giving, and by that alone does he become happy hereafter.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that hoarding leads nowhere good, while giving brings lasting happiness.
buddhism.tie_back: Giving turns passing wealth into lasting benefit, which is what the Kural urges.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good match on generosity as the right use of wealth; the verse does not state wealth's impermanence as the reason.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The poor old couple Baucis and Philemon gladly share their meagre food and wine with two disguised strangers who turn out to be Zeus and Hermes; the gods save them from a flood and turn their hut into a temple.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid's tale rewards a couple who used what little they had for hospitality right away, without holding back.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Giving at once from what you have, rather than clinging to it, is the Kural's instruction for using unstable wealth.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase and weak match: a hospitality story with no explicit teaching on the impermanence of wealth. A Roman retelling of Greek myth, used as the best available fit.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Lady Philosophy asks Boethius whether riches are precious by their own nature, and argues that money shines more brightly when it is spent on others than when it is hoarded, since avarice makes people hated and generosity makes them honoured.
philosophy.explanation: In Boethius' dialogue, Philosophy shows that wealth only has real value when it is given away.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts say the only good use of passing wealth is to put it at once into generous action.
philosophy.source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book II, prose 5
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Moderate match: Boethius argues that giving is better than hoarding and that fortune's gifts are unstable, but he does not frame it as an urgent moral duty.

kurals.tamil:
நாளென ஒன்றுபோற் காட்டி உயிர்ஈரும்
வாளது உணர்வார்ப் பெறின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Naal ena ondru pol kaatti uyir eerum
Vaal adhu unarvaar perin.
kurals.meaning: The day presents itself as a simple unit of time, but to those who understand, it is really a saw that cuts away at life.
kurals.elementary: Each day feels like just another day: you wake up, play, and sleep. But every day that passes is one less day you have left, like a saw slowly cutting through a log. This kural says wise people notice this.
kurals.university: The couplet turns on an unmasking: “naal” (the day) displays itself (kaatti) as a neutral thing, an ordinary measure of time, but its real nature is a “vaal” (blade, commonly understood as a saw) that “eerum” (cleaves, saws through) life. The verb eer suggests the slow back-and-forth of a saw rather than a single cut, so life is shown being worn away in daily strokes. The conditional “unarvaarp perin” (if one finds those who understand) implies that such people are rare; most take the passing day at face value. Philosophically the kural anticipates Seneca's remark that we die daily and the Psalmist's prayer to ‘number our days’: time is not a container in which life takes place, but the very process by which life is used up.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bhartrhari laments that with every rising and setting of the sun, life is shortened day by day, yet people, busy with their many affairs, do not notice time slipping away.
hinduism.explanation: The poet observes that each passing day quietly takes something off a person's lifespan.
hinduism.tie_back: This is almost the Kural's own image: the ordinary day, marked by sunrise and sunset, is secretly cutting away at life.
hinduism.source: Bhartrhari, Vairagyashataka (verse beginning ādityasya gatāgatair; numbering varies by edition)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Very close thematic parallel (daily erosion of life by the sun's cycle); verse numbering differs across editions, so the exact number was not fixed.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away.”
christianity.explanation: James reminds his readers that life is a brief vapour and tomorrow is never guaranteed.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts correct the illusion that time is plentiful: life is being used up day by day.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong on the brevity of life; the Kural's specific image of the day as a saw has no direct equivalent.

islam.quote_or_event: “By time, Indeed, mankind is in loss, Except for those who have believed and done righteous deeds and advised each other to truth and advised each other to patience.”
islam.explanation: Surat al-Asr swears by time and declares that people are in loss as time passes, unless they fill it with faith and good deeds.
islam.tie_back: Time as a steady loss of life is the Kural's point; al-Asr adds the remedy the chapter goes on to give: good deeds.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match: time itself as the measure of human loss.

judaism.quote_or_event: “So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.”
judaism.explanation: The Psalm asks God to help people count their days so they grow wise.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's ‘those who understand’ are exactly those who have learned to number their days.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match: awareness of each day's passing is treated as the beginning of wisdom.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Just as a cowherd drives the cattle to pasture with a staff, so do old age and death drive the life force of beings (from existence to existence).
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha pictures aging and death steadily driving life onward, as a herdsman drives cattle with a stick.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts show time as an active force wearing life away, not a harmless backdrop.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good match on time as an agent consuming life; the image (cowherd rather than saw) differs.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod names the three Fates, Clotho, Lachesis and Atropos, who spin, measure out and finally cut the thread of each mortal life.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Greek myth, every life is a thread that is spun, measured, and in the end cut by Atropos, ‘the one who cannot be turned’.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Fates' shears and the Kural's saw both picture time as a blade working on the length of a life.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. The spin/measure/cut roles are later Greek tradition built on Hesiod's names. Good imagery match, but the Fates cut once at the end, whereas the Kural's saw cuts daily.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “What man can you show me who places any value on his time, who reckons the worth of each day, who understands that he is dying daily?”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca tells Lucilius that most people waste their days without noticing that each one is a part of their death already lived.
philosophy.tie_back: Seneca's ‘dying daily’ is the Kural's day-saw, and his rare person who ‘understands’ matches Valluvar's ‘those who understand’.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 1.2 (Gummere translation)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match: the ordinary day as a hidden unit of dying, recognised only by the few who understand.

kurals.tamil:
நாச்செற்று விக்குள்மேல் வாராமுன் நல்வினை
மேற்சென்று செய்யப் படும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Naachchetru vikkul mel vaaraamun nalvinai
Mersendru seyyap padum.
kurals.meaning: Before the tongue is stilled and the death rattle rises in the throat, hurry to do good deeds.
kurals.elementary: If you want to say sorry or help someone, don't wait for ‘someday’, because someday might not come. This kural says do your good deeds now, while you still can talk and act.
kurals.university: Valluvar gives the chapter's abstract point a stark physical image: “naa chetru” (the tongue locked or stilled) and “vikkul mel vaaraa mun” (before the hiccup, the death rattle, rises), which are the classical signs of the last moments of life. The imperative “mersendru” (going forward, pressing ahead) carries the sense of taking the initiative and not waiting for circumstances. The image of a silenced tongue also implies that at the end one cannot even speak one's intentions, let alone carry them out. The kural thus moves from recognising impermanence to acting urgently, an ethic of timeliness found in Rabbi Eliezer's ‘repent one day before your death’, the Quran's warning against wishing for a reprieve at death, and Marcus Aurelius' ‘while it is in thy power, be good’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Those who relinquish the body while remembering Me at the moment of death will come to Me. There is certainly no doubt about this.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that a person's state of mind at death shapes what follows, which implies preparing throughout life for that moment.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts treat the moment of death as decisive and urge preparation well before it arrives.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Moderate match: the Gita focuses on remembrance of God at death, the Kural on performing good deeds before it.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I must work the works of him that sent me, while it is day: the night cometh, when no man can work.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus says good works must be done while there is still daylight, because night is coming when no one can work.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's silenced tongue is Jesus' ‘night’: the point after which good deeds can no longer be done.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close structural parallel: do good now, before an approaching end makes action impossible.

islam.quote_or_event: “And spend [in the way of Allah] from what We have provided you before death approaches one of you and he says, "My Lord, if only You would delay me for a brief term so I would give charity and be among the righteous."”
islam.explanation: The Quran urges believers to give now, before death comes and they beg in vain for a little more time to do good.
islam.tie_back: The same urgency: act before the final moment, when the chance to do good is gone.
islam._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match: do good deeds before death arrives, since regret at the end is useless.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Eliezer said: ... And repent one day before your death.”
judaism.explanation: Since no one knows the day of their death, the Talmud explains, this means repenting every day.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts tell people to act before death while hiding its date, so the only safe time is now.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 2:10 (Mishnah Yomit, trans. Joshua Kulp)
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close: urgency before an unknown hour of death; Avot speaks of repentance, the Kural of good deeds.

buddhism.quote_or_event: For him who is assailed by death there is no protection by kinsmen. None there are to save him — no sons, nor father, nor relatives. Realizing this fact, let the wise man, restrained by morality, hasten to clear the path leading to Nibbana.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells the wise to hurry along the moral path, since nothing can protect a person once death arrives.
buddhism.tie_back: ‘Hasten’ is the Kural's ‘mersendru’: the certainty of death is a reason to act on the good without delay.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close match on urgency grounded in death; the Buddhist goal is Nibbana rather than merit alone.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Say not a word in death's favour; I would rather be a paid servant in a poor man's house and be above ground than king of kings among the dead.”
greek_mythology.explanation: In the underworld the great hero Achilles tells Odysseus that even the humblest living life is better than glory among the dead, where nothing more can be done.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Achilles' regret shows why the Kural insists on acting now: once life ends, no deed remains possible.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Partial match: it stresses the value of life before death, not the doing of good deeds; used as the best Greek mythic parallel.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Do not act as if thou wert going to live ten thousand years. Death hangs over thee. While thou livest, while it is in thy power, be good.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius reminds himself that death is always near, so the time to be good is now.
philosophy.tie_back: ‘While it is in thy power’ matches the Kural's ‘before the tongue is stilled’: goodness must be done while one still can.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match in both logic and urgency.

kurals.tamil:
நெருநல் உளனொருவன் இன்றில்லை என்னும்
பெருமை உடைத்துஇவ் வுலகு.
kurals.transliteration:
Nerunal ulan oruvan indru illai ennum
Perumai udaiththu ivvulagu.
kurals.meaning: This world has the ‘greatness’ of being a place where someone who was here yesterday is gone today.
kurals.elementary: Sometimes we hear, ‘I just saw him yesterday, and now he's gone.’ This kural says that is simply how the world works: people can be here one day and gone the next.
kurals.university: The couplet is famous for its irony. “Perumai” (greatness, glory) is normally praise, but Valluvar awards it to the world for the most unsettling of distinctions, that a man alive “nerunal” (yesterday) is not there “indru” (today). Commentators such as the thirukkural-thamizh gloss explicitly read perumai here as a mocking word for the world's instability. The unit of time is only a single day, which heightens the sense of suddenness. The world's one reliable ‘achievement’ is the constant disappearance of its inhabitants. The observation echoes the Yaksha's question in the Mahabharata about the wonder of human denial of death, and Marcus Aurelius' remark about yesterday's mucus becoming tomorrow's ashes.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Asked by the Yaksha what is the most wonderful thing in the world, Yudhishthira answers that every day countless beings go to the abode of Yama, yet those who remain act as though they will live forever.
hinduism.explanation: In the Mahabharata, the wisest of the Pandavas names humanity's denial of death, in the face of daily deaths, as the greatest wonder.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's ‘greatness’ of a world where yesterday's man is gone today is the same ironic wonder Yudhishthira points to.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Aranyaka (Vana) Parva, Yaksha Prashna (ch. 313 in Ganguli's numbering)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Very close: daily deaths set against human blindness, framed as an ironic ‘wonder’, just as the Kural uses ‘greatness’.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For all flesh is as grass, and all the glory of man as the flower of grass. The grass withereth, and the flower thereof falleth away:”
christianity.explanation: Peter, quoting Isaiah, says human life and glory wither like grass and flowers.
christianity.tie_back: Peter speaks of the ‘glory of man’ withering; the Kural ironically calls the world's constant loss its ‘glory’.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on fleeting human life and the irony of ‘glory’; the Kural's one-day timescale is sharper.

islam.quote_or_event: “Every soul will taste death, and you will only be given your [full] compensation on the Day of Resurrection. ... And what is the life of this world except the enjoyment of delusion.”
islam.explanation: The Quran states that every living soul will die and that worldly life is a deceptive enjoyment.
islam.tie_back: Both texts present death as the world's universal and reliable feature, which exposes the world's promise of permanence as a delusion.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on universality of death; lacks the Kural's yesterday/today suddenness.

judaism.quote_or_event: “As for man, his days are as grass: as a flower of the field, so he flourisheth. For the wind passeth over it, and it is gone; and the place thereof shall know it no more.”
judaism.explanation: The Psalm says a person flourishes like a wildflower, then a wind passes and they are gone, and even their place forgets them.
judaism.tie_back: ‘It is gone, and the place thereof shall know it no more’ is the Kural's ‘here yesterday, not here today’.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close: sudden disappearance, with the world carrying on as if the person had not been there.

buddhism.quote_or_event: As a mighty flood sweeps away the sleeping village, so death carries away the person of distracted mind who only plucks the flowers (of pleasure).
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares death to a sudden flood that sweeps away a sleeping village overnight.
buddhism.tie_back: Overnight disappearance is the Kural's image: those present yesterday are swept away by today.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good match on the suddenness of death; the verse also criticises the distracted, which the Kural leaves implicit.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Men come and go as leaves year by year upon the trees. Those of autumn the wind sheds upon the ground, but when spring returns the forest buds forth with fresh ones. Even so is it with the generations of mankind, the new spring up as the old are passing away.”
greek_mythology.explanation: On the battlefield, Glaucus tells Diomedes that human generations fall and replace one another like leaves.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The world's constant coming and going of people, which the Kural wryly calls its ‘greatness’, is Homer's falling of leaves.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong thematic match on human transience; Homer's timescale is generational, the Kural's a single day.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Always observe how ephemeral and worthless human things are, and what was yesterday a little mucus to-morrow will be a mummy or ashes.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius reminds himself how quickly human life passes from beginning to end.
philosophy.tie_back: Marcus' ‘yesterday ... to-morrow’ matches the Kural's ‘yesterday ... today’, both stressing how short the interval is.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close match in both theme and day-to-day framing.

kurals.tamil:
ஒருபொழுதும் வாழ்வது அறியார் கருதுப
கோடியும் அல்ல பல.
kurals.transliteration:
Oru pozhudhum vaazhvadhu ariyaar karudhupa
Kodiyum alla pala.
kurals.meaning: People who cannot know whether they will live even one more moment still make plans beyond counting, more than ten million.
kurals.elementary: Someone might plan what they'll do next week, next year, and in ten years, even though nobody knows for sure what will happen tomorrow. This kural gently laughs at how many plans we make when we can't even be sure of the next hour.
kurals.university: The couplet's force comes from the mismatch of scale: “oru pozhudhu” (a single moment or watch of the day) against “kodiyum alla pala” (not a crore, i.e. ten million, but more). People who cannot guarantee a single stretch of time still carry countless projects, desires and calculations. Commentators note the progression within the chapter from “yesterday/today” (336) to an even smaller unit, “one moment” (337), tightening the frame of uncertainty. The critique is not of planning as such but of a mind that lives in imagined futures while forgetting its own fragility. The Gita's portrait of the deluded man counting his gains ‘today’ and ‘tomorrow’, Jesus' parable of the rich fool, and Aeschylus' ‘blind hopes’ all diagnose the same condition.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The demoniac persons think, "I have gained so much wealth today, and I shall now fulfill this desire of mine. This is mine, and tomorrow I shall have even more."”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes deluded people who endlessly plan their gains for today and tomorrow, as though their lives were secure.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's ‘more than ten million’ calculations, made by people who cannot be sure of the next moment.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong match on endless worldly scheming; the Gita frames it as demonic arrogance, while the Kural frames it as ignorance of mortality.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And I will say to my soul, Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry. But God said unto him, Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?”
christianity.explanation: In Jesus' parable, a rich man plans years of comfort and dies that very night.
christianity.tie_back: The rich fool is the Kural's planner: many years of plans, not even one secure night.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one narrative match of long-range plans set against a life that ends that night.

islam.quote_or_event: “And no soul perceives what it will earn tomorrow, and no soul perceives in what land it will die.”
islam.explanation: The Quran states that no one knows what tomorrow will bring or where they will die.
islam.tie_back: Both texts point to the basic uncertainty of the future that makes endless planning foolish.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on uncertainty of the next day and of death; lacks the Kural's satire of countless plans.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Boast not thyself of to morrow; for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs warns against confident talk about tomorrow, since no one knows what a single day will bring.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts set human certainty about the future against ignorance of even one day ahead.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close match on the arrogance of planning an unknown future.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Here shall I live during the rains, here in winter and summer” — thus thinks the fool. He does not realize the danger (that death might intervene).
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha pictures a fool making plans for every season without realising death may come first.
buddhism.tie_back: The fool's seasonal planning is the Kural's ‘more than ten million’ thoughts in someone unsure of a single moment.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match: long-range planning by one who ignores the nearness of death.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “I caused mortals to cease foreseeing their doom. ... I caused blind hopes to dwell within their breasts.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Prometheus says he stopped humans from foreseeing their deaths by giving them ‘blind hopes’.
greek_mythology.tie_back: In both texts, people forget how fragile life is and fill their minds with countless hopes and plans.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good match on the psychology of unmindful hope; Aeschylus presents it partly as a mercy, the Kural as folly.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca tells Paulinus that people live as if destined to live forever, never thinking of their own frailty or of how much time has already gone, and put off real living to their fiftieth or sixtieth year.
philosophy.explanation: In On the Shortness of Life, Seneca criticises people who put off living and make distant plans while forgetting that they are mortal.
philosophy.tie_back: Seneca's forgetful planners are the Kural's people who cannot secure one moment yet plan without end.
philosophy.source: Seneca, On the Shortness of Life (De Brevitate Vitae) 3
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase (English translations differ; exact wording not locked to one edition). Very close thematic match.

kurals.tamil:
குடம்பை தனித்துஒழியப் புள்பறந் தற்றே
உடம்பொடு உயிரிடை நட்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Kudambai thaniththu ozhiyap pul parandhatre
Udambodu uyiridai natpu.
kurals.meaning: The bond between body and soul is like that of a bird and the egg (or nest) it leaves behind, empty and alone, when it flies away.
kurals.elementary: A baby bird grows inside an egg, but one day it breaks out and flies off, leaving the empty shell behind. This kural says our life and our body are like that: one day life flies off, and the body is left behind like the shell.
kurals.university: The meaning turns on the word “kudambai”, which Parimelazhagar and many commentators gloss as ‘egg’ (so the chick breaks out and leaves the shell), while others read it as ‘nest’ (so a grown bird abandons its home); both readings agree that the container is left “thaniththu ozhiya” (abandoned, alone). Calling the relationship “natpu” (friendship) is pointed, since it is a friendship of convenience that ends the moment the occupant departs. The egg reading adds the idea that the body was the soul's place of formation, not its permanent home, which prepares for kural 340. The image of soul and body as distinct, one of them leaving the other, parallels the Gita's worn-out garments, Ecclesiastes' spirit returning to God, and Plato's definition of death in the Phaedo as the separation of soul from body.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “As a person sheds worn-out garments and wears new ones, likewise, at the time of death, the soul casts off its worn-out body and enters a new one.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna explains that the soul discards the body at death as one discards old clothes.
hinduism.tie_back: In both images the soul leaves and the body is left behind like an empty covering: garments in the Gita, shell or nest in the Kural.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close structural match: the soul departs and its bodily container is abandoned.

christianity.quote_or_event: “We are confident, I say, and willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord.”
christianity.explanation: Paul speaks of leaving the body behind at death to be with Christ.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts see the body as something the self eventually leaves, not the self's permanent place.
christianity._accuracy_note: Moderate: shared soul/body separation, but Paul's tone is hopeful longing, whereas the Kural's is detached observation. Christian doctrine also affirms bodily resurrection.

islam.quote_or_event: “No! When the soul has reached the collar bones ... And the dying one is certain that it is the [time of] separation”
islam.explanation: The Quran describes the soul rising in the dying body, and the dying person knowing it is time for separation.
islam.tie_back: ‘Separation’ (al-firaq) is the Kural's parting of bird and shell, soul and body.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on death as soul-body separation; no bird or egg image.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it.”
judaism.explanation: Ecclesiastes describes death as the body returning to dust and the spirit returning to God.
judaism.tie_back: Body and spirit part ways at death: the body stays behind like the Kural's empty shell, while the spirit goes on.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close match on the parting of body and spirit, with the body left behind.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Ere long, alas! this body will lie upon the earth, unheeded and lifeless, like a useless log.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha reminds his followers that the body will soon lie lifeless and ignored, like a discarded log.
buddhism.tie_back: The abandoned body, left alone and useless, is the Kural's deserted shell or nest.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good match on the abandoned body; Buddhism denies a permanent departing soul (anatta), so the ‘bird’ half does not map directly.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Patroclus is struck down by Hector, his soul leaves his limbs and flies down to the house of Hades, mourning its fate and the youth and strength it leaves behind.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer pictures the psyche flying out of the body at the moment of death.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The soul flying away and leaving the body behind is the Kural's bird deserting its shell.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase (exact Butler wording not locked). Strong image match: the soul flies from the body; Homer's shade grieves, while the Kural is detached.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “And is this anything but the separation of soul and body? And being dead is the attainment of this separation; when the soul exists in herself, and is parted from the body and the body is parted from the soul-that is death?”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates defines death as the soul and the body parting from each other.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato's definition is the philosophical form of the Kural's image: two companions whose ‘friendship’ ends when one departs.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close conceptual match: death defined as the separation of soul and body.

kurals.tamil:
உறங்கு வதுபோலுஞ் சாக்காடு உறங்கி
விழிப்பது போலும் பிறப்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Urangu vadhu polum saakkaadu urangi
Vizhippadhu polum pirappu.
kurals.meaning: Death is like falling asleep, and birth is like waking up after sleep.
kurals.elementary: Every night you fall asleep, and every morning you wake up again. This kural says dying is like falling asleep, and being born is like waking up.
kurals.university: The couplet is the chapter's most compressed statement: “saakkaadu” (death) is like “uranguvadhu” (sleeping), and “pirappu” (birth) is like “urangi vizhippadhu” (waking after sleep). Most traditional commentators read it within the Indian framework of rebirth: death and birth follow one another as naturally as sleep and waking, so the cycle is familiar rather than terrifying, and the real goal is to escape it (veedu). Some modern readers, including Kalaignar's gloss, take a more secular line, stressing that death is a sleep from which one does not wake. The analogy is found across traditions: the Greek twins Hypnos and Thanatos, Socrates' ‘dreamless sleep’, the biblical ‘those who sleep in the dust’ shall awake, and the Quran's teaching that God takes souls both in death and in sleep.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Death is certain for one who has been born, and rebirth is inevitable for one who has died. Therefore, you should not lament over the inevitable.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that death and rebirth follow each other as surely as night and day.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's sleep-and-waking cycle is the Gita's cycle of death and rebirth.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong match on the death-birth cycle; the Gita does not use the sleep image here.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Our friend Lazarus sleepeth; but I go, that I may awake him out of sleep.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus speaks of the dead Lazarus as asleep and of raising him as waking him.
christianity.tie_back: Death as sleep and return to life as waking is exactly the Kural's pair of images.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong verbal match on the sleep/wake metaphor; the context is resurrection by Christ, not a natural cycle of rebirth.

islam.quote_or_event: “Allah takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that do not die [He takes] during their sleep. Then He keeps those for which He has decreed death and releases the others for a specified term.”
islam.explanation: The Quran teaches that sleep and death are the same kind of event: in both, God takes the soul, returning it only to those who wake.
islam.tie_back: Both texts see sleep and death as closely related, and waking as a return of life.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close: sleep and death are explicitly equated as the taking of the soul. Islam does not teach rebirth, so the ‘birth as waking’ half maps only to resurrection.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.”
judaism.explanation: Daniel speaks of the dead as sleepers in the dust who will one day wake.
judaism.tie_back: The same metaphor: death as sleep and a return to life as waking.
judaism._accuracy_note: Clear use of the sleep/wake metaphor for death and resurrection; not a cycle of repeated births as in the Kural.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Long is the night to the sleepless; long is the league to the weary. Long is worldly existence to fools who know not the Sublime Truth.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha likens the long round of births and deaths (samsara) to a long night for those who do not understand the Dhamma.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts use night and sleep imagery for the round of birth and death.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Weak match: samsara is compared to a long night, but the verse does not equate death with sleep or birth with waking. Used as the best available Dhammapada parallel.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod makes Hypnos (Sleep) and Thanatos (Death) the twin children of Night, dwelling together at the edge of the world: Sleep gentle to men, Death with a heart of iron.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Greek myth, Sleep and Death are brothers, twin sons of Night.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Making Sleep and Death twins is the mythic form of the Kural's claim that death is like sleep.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Strong kinship of sleep and death; the Greek myth has no ‘birth as waking’ counterpart.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “... but a sleep like the sleep of him who is undisturbed even by the sight of dreams, death will be an unspeakable gain.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates tells his jurors that if death is like a dreamless sleep, it is nothing to fear and may even be a gain.
philosophy.tie_back: Socrates and the Kural both remove death's terror by comparing it to ordinary sleep.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close on death-as-sleep; Socrates also offers an alternative (migration of the soul), and does not describe birth as waking.

kurals.tamil:
புக்கில் அமைந்தின்று கொல்லோ உடம்பினுள்
துச்சில் இருந்த உயிர்க்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Pukkil amaindhindru kollo udambinul
Thuchchil irundha uyirkku.
kurals.meaning: It seems that the soul, which only lodges for a while in a corner of the body, has not yet found a permanent home of its own.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a traveller who keeps staying in borrowed rooms, moving from one to the next, never having a house of their own. This kural says the soul is like that traveller: the body is only a temporary room, and it is still looking for its true home.
kurals.university: Valluvar closes the chapter with a question rather than a statement. “Pukkil” (a settled dwelling, a home one enters to stay) is contrasted with “thuchchil” (a temporary lodging, a borrowed corner), and the particle “kollo” (is it perhaps that...?) gives the line a tone of wondering. The soul is pictured as a tenant in a rented corner of the body, which explains why it keeps moving from body to body: it has not yet reached its true home, which traditional commentators identify with veedu (liberation). The chapter thus moves from wealth (332-333), to time (334-337), to the body (338-339), and finally to the homelessness of the soul, handing on to the next chapter on renunciation. Parallels include the Gita's ‘transient world’ from which liberated souls do not return, Paul's ‘earthly house of this tabernacle’, the hadith of being a ‘stranger or traveller’, and Marcus Aurelius' ‘stranger's sojourn’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Having attained Me, the great souls are no more subject to rebirth in this world, which is transient and full of misery, because they have attained the highest perfection.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that the soul keeps returning to this impermanent world until it reaches God, its final home.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's lodger who has not yet found a home is the soul still in this transient world; the Gita names the home it seeks.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong match on the world and body as temporary lodgings and a final abode beyond them; the Kural only hints at that abode.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For we know that if our earthly house of this tabernacle were dissolved, we have a building of God, an house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.”
christianity.explanation: Paul calls the body a temporary tent, contrasted with the eternal home God provides.
christianity.tie_back: The body as a tent (tabernacle) rather than a permanent house is the Kural's ‘thuchchil’ versus ‘pukkil’.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close: the body is a temporary dwelling and the soul's true home lies elsewhere.

islam.quote_or_event: “Be in this world as if you were a stranger or a traveler.” Ibn `Umar used to say, “If you survive till the evening, do not expect to be alive in the morning.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet tells Ibn Umar to live in this world like a stranger or traveller passing through.
islam.tie_back: The traveller who has not settled is the Kural's soul lodging in a borrowed corner, with no permanent home here.
islam._accuracy_note: Close: a temporary, homeless state in this world; the hadith applies it to worldly life generally rather than to the soul in the body.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For we are strangers before thee, and sojourners, as were all our fathers: our days on the earth are as a shadow, and there is none abiding.”
judaism.explanation: King David prays that humans are strangers and temporary residents on earth, with no lasting place.
judaism.tie_back: ‘Sojourners’ with ‘none abiding’ matches the Kural's soul as a temporary lodger without a settled home.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close: human existence as temporary sojourn with no abiding place.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Through many a birth in samsara have I wandered in vain, seeking the builder of this house (of life). Repeated birth is indeed suffering! O house-builder, you are seen! You will not build this house again.
buddhism.explanation: At his awakening, the Buddha describes wandering through countless births, each a new ‘house’, until he ends the cycle.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts picture life moving from one temporary house to another without a lasting home, and point to an end of that wandering.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong image match (body as house, restless wandering through births); Buddhism rejects a permanent soul, so the ‘lodger’ is interpreted differently.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After the fall of Troy, Odysseus wanders for ten years, lodging as a guest or captive in one strange place after another and longing for his home in Ithaca.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Odyssey is the story of a man who stays everywhere but belongs nowhere until he finally reaches home.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus as a guest in foreign houses loosely mirrors the Kural's soul lodging in a body while seeking its true home.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase and loose, allegorical match only: later Neoplatonist readers took Odysseus' voyage as the soul's journey, but Homer's story is literal.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Everything which belongs to the body is a stream, and what belongs to the soul is a dream and vapour, and life is a warfare and a stranger's sojourn, and after-fame is oblivion.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius calls life a stranger's temporary stay, with the body constantly flowing away.
philosophy.tie_back: ‘A stranger's sojourn’ is almost the Kural's image of the soul as a temporary lodger in the body.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close match on life as temporary lodging; Marcus is agnostic about the soul's final home.
